set.p: Time supposed to be occupied, From the noon of the first day to the afternoon of the second.

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: Lord Wilmot's Apartment in St. James's.—A Breakfast-table laid out.

sp.speaker: SMART
sp.p: Just on the stroke of twelve, and my Lord not risen. He never wants sleep more than once a week,—but when he does sleep, he sleeps as he does every thing else—better than any man in the three kingdoms. Well, he is a merry fine gentleman, to be sure; so kind-hearted and generous; but, lauk, if one judged by his words, and not by his actions, one would say he was the wickedest dog that—Mum!

div.stage: Enter Lord Wilmot, in his dressing-gown, from side-door.

sp.speaker: WILMOT
sp.p: “And sleepless lovers just at twelve—awake!” That little fellow Pope hits us off to a hair. Smart, my chocolate. Any duels to-day? I forget—

sp.speaker: SMART
sp.p: No, my Lord, no duels. Only three drums, four routs, five dinners, and six suppers.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Is that all? Dull day before me. Not worth getting up for. Smart, you have now lived with me six months; pray, what do you think of me?

sp.speaker: SMART.
sp.p: Oh, my Lord, I think there's not another gentleman in the world like your Lordship—

sp.speaker: WILMOT
sp.p: Take care! I discharged your predecessor for flattery! Go on, and let me see how you get out of that dangerous exordium.

sp.speaker: SMART.
sp.p: Yes, my Lord! not a gentleman like you for speaking ill of yourself and doing good to another.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: This knave has been bribed by my enemies to ruin my character. Doing good to another, you scandalous libeller! Am I not renowned from Soho to the Mall as a headlong— immoveable—reckless—phlegmatical—true King of the Mode—frigid as Diogenes the Cynic—and fiery as Timour the Tartar? Learn how the wits of our day represent, on the stage, a fine gentleman; and beware how you disparage your master.

sp.speaker: SMART
sp.p: What hard words he does give himself! If hard words could break bones, I would not be in his skin for something.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: What is this note? The hand is unknown. Pshaw! the hand of a woman! It must wait with the rest. Ladies' letters don't cool—man's chocolate does.
The Frenchman implies that a good digestion is the sign of a bad heart. What a heart I must have! Could digest an anvil!

sp.speaker: SMART.
sp.p: I beg pardon, my Lord; but that note was left by the lady herself.

sp.speaker: WILMOT
sp.p: Oh! young and pretty, of course! Heart not moved in the least! Petrified!

sp.speaker: SMART.
sp.p: She wore the mask ladies sometimes wear, when they go out alone; but I don't think she was very young. She seemed in great distress of mind, for when she gave me the letter, her hand trembled so, that—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Distress, you blockhead; why the deuce did not you say that before?

“I pray you, my Lord, to forgive this intrusion —noticed you calling at the house of Sir Geoffrey Thornside —[Ha!]—seen you walking in the garden with Mistress Lucy, his daughter—[Hum!]—heard you had rescued that young lady from danger—[What gossip!]—many stories have reached me attesting the honour of your character and the kindness of your heart—[Stuff; where's my purse?] venture with reluctance to entreat you would honour me with a visit; you could render an inestimable service—perform a most benevolent action—[Wonder if there's eno' in the purse!]— for reasons I cannot explain, would not wish your Lordship to be seen entering my house; therefore, if you grant my request, —any hour in the evening, after dusk—beg your Lordship not to mention the contents of this letter—to Sir Geoffrey—his daughter—to any one; strictly confidential—for same reasons, cannot give you my name—must be content with subjoining my address,—Crown and Portcullis, Deadman's Lane—”Deadman's Lane! It must be a churchyard, and the writer a ghost! Smart, are you too lively to know a place on this earth or below it—called Deadman's Lane?

sp.speaker: SMART.
sp.p: Yes, my Lord; it is at the back of Sir Geoffrey Thornside's.
Is your Lordship at home?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Yes;—see who it is.
Very strange letter!— in meaning mysterious—in direction funereal. I will call; were it only for the sweet name of Lucy that I kiss here in effigy! Oh, that divine, innocent charming Lucy!

sp.speaker: SMART.
sp.p: Mr. Shadowly Softhead.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Softhead, my imitator, my double—who cuts his cloth (his father's a clothier) according to the coat of a Lord; and sets his puny constitution against my frame of a Hercules. The best little man in the world!—ambitious to be thought good for nothing;—upset by a wine-glass, and frightened out of his wits by a petticoat!—
Ha, Softhead! my Pylades—my second self! Animæ—

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Enemy!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Dimidium meæ.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Dimi! that's the oath last in fashion, I warrant.
sp.stage: (With a swagger and a slap on the back.)
sp.p: Dimidum meæ, how d'ye do?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: But what a fellow you are! Slunk off last night at the third bottle. I thought you were a staunch Bacchanalian.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: So I am! staunch to the bone. But I say, don't you sometimes feel rather qualmy the next morning?—queerish and headachy—a sort of uppish, downish, all-overish Bacchanalian sensation!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: I?—never! Oh, if you are capable of such vulgar infirmities after a miserable third bottle or so, never think of living with us: we Lords of Misrule are all made of iron, like the man in Spenser's Fairy Queen.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: And so am I—iron! Nothing ever ails me! I only asked from curiosity—I could have sate you all out; but—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Ah, I take it, an assignation! Softhead, you know you're a monster.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: A monster! Are you a monster?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Ay, horrible.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Dimidum meæ, and so am I!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: As we grow seasoned, 'tis astonishing how much we require. Wine has now no effect upon me! I think of taking to aquafortis. We'll have a bout of it some day. Aqua-fortis! Vigorous fellows, like Sir John Bruin, Colonel Flint, Lord Strongbow, me, and—yourself, could carry off a gallon a-piece!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Charming!—Excellent!—Aqua-fortis, I'm a dead man!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: As for women, they are duller than wine. A mere harmless gallantry has no longer a charm for me.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Nor for me either!—
Never had.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Nothing should excite us true men of pleasure but some colossal atrocity, to bring our necks within an inch of the gallows!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: He's a perfect demon! Alas, I shall never come up to his mark!

sp.speaker: SMART.
sp.p: Mr. Hardman, my lord.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Hush! Must not shock Mr. Hardman, the most friendly obliging man, and so clever—will be a minister some day. But not one of our set.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Oh, I've often heard of Mr. Hardman. We visit at the same house; the rising member of parliament?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Rising, yes! Pray what did he rise from? Do you know his origin?

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: He's like the Sibyl of Cuma. Knows all about every one; and nobody knows aught about him.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Is that like a Sibyl of Cuma? La! there are plenty such Sibyls in London!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: And how fares my dear Lord?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Bravely—and you? Ah! you men who live for others have a hard life of it. Let me present to you my friend, Mr. Shadowly Softhead.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: The son of the great clothier who has such weight in the Guild? I have heard of you from Mr. Easy and others, though never so fortunate as to meet you before, Mr. Softhead.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Shadowly Softhead:—my grandmother was one of the Shadowlys—a genteel family that move about Court. She married a Softhead,—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: A race much esteemed in the city.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Esteemed in the city! The Softheads? No race has more votes for it! Your father's the head of that House; a most valuable man! Ah, my Lord! these are critical times: we can't disguise from ourselves that the Jacobites are daring and numerous. Our great Prime Minister needs all the support he can get. You 've no notion, Lord Wilmot, how Sir Robert Walpole esteems you.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Indeed I have: just like myself! One always esteems a thing—before one has bought it.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: A sorry joke, Mr. Softhead—I've known him more witty. A new picture, my Lord? I'm no very great judge—but it seems to me quite a master-piece.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: I've a passion for art. Sold off my stud to buy that picture.
And please my poor father.) 'Tis a Murillo.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: A Murillo! you know that Walpole, too, has a passion for pictures.—In despair at this moment that he can't find a Murillo to hang up in his gallery. If ever you want to corrupt the Prime Minister's virtue, you have only to say, “I have got a Murillo.”

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Well, if, instead of the pictures, he'll just hang up the men he has bought, you may tell him he shall have my Murillo for nothing!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Bought! now really, my Lord, this is so vulgar a scandal against Sir Robert. Let me assure your Lordship—

sp.speaker: WILMOT
sp.p: Nay, it needs not, dear Hardman; the best proof of a Minister's merits is in the zeal and attachment of men like yourself.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: I thank you, my Lord.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: But prithee, dear Hardman, where left you your cloak?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Cloak? Outside the door.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Then, outside with the cloak, leave my Lord and your Lordship. Plague on these titles among friends. My Lord with the world; Wilmot with my comrades; Frederick at my father's home; and plain Fred in my bachelor's lodgings.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: And I live to call a man Fred, who's called my Lord by the world! Oh, sir, you don't know my friend Fred as we do. Does he, Fred?

sp.speaker: WILMOT
sp.p: Hum. I'm not sure that two diminutives go well together. But as for titles and all such tedious ceremonials, they die in the air that hallows these rooms to the freedom of youth, and the equality of friendship. And if the Duke of Middlesex himself—commonly styled “the Proud Duke”—who said to his Duchess, when she astonished his dignity one day with a kiss, “Madam, my first wife was a Percy, and she never took such a liberty;—”

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Ha! ha! well, if “the Proud Duke”—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Could deign to come here, we would say, “How d'ye do, my dear Middlesex!”

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: So we would, Fred! Middlesex.—Shouldn't you like to know a Duke, Mr. Hardman?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: I have known one or two—in opposition; and had rather too much of 'em.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Too much of a Duke! La! I could never have eno' of a Duke!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: You may live to think otherwise. But, my dear Wilmot, you will soon have occasion for that well-bred familiarity with which you threaten his Grace; for, as I left Lockett's, I saw the Duke stepping into his carriage and heard his lackies order the coachman to drive to your lodgings,— stopping first at Bygrave's the gunsmith—
who is suspected of selling arms to the malcontents.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Ha! The proud Duke!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: And that's one reason why I came hither. I would know what mischief that Jacobite Duke is devising—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: No, it will never do! Smart, I say—not at home!
Confound it!—too late—the Duke's in the hall!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: But you'll not be so absurd as to do what you boasted!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Not! If a man with notions of honour not larger than would cover the point of a pin were to boast that he would put the Monument into his pocket—why he must pocket the Monument, or throw himself from the top of it.

sp.speaker: SMART.
sp.p: His Grace the Duke of Middlesex.

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: My Lord Wilmot, your most obedient servant.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Now then, courage! How d'ye do, my dear Middlesex?

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: “How d'ye do?” “Middlesex!” Gracious heaven! what will this age come to?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: Well, it may be the fashion,—yet I could hardly advise you to adopt it.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: But if Fred—

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Oh! certainly Fred is an excellent model—

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Yet, there's something very awful in a live Duke!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Tut! a mere mortal like ourselves, after all.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: D'ye really think so?—upon your honour?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Sir, I am sure of it,—upon my honour, a mortal!

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.stage: (turning stiffly round, and half rising from his chair in majestic condescension).
sp.p: Your Lordship's friends? A good day to you, gentlemen!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: And a good day to yourself. My Lord Du—I mean, my dear boy!—Middlesex, how d'ye do?

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: Mid!—Boy!—sex!—dear!—my head is confused. I must be in a dream,—certainly a hideous dream. And that small man is the nightmare! He is coming this way!—Powers above!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: He looks rather puzzled. Taking snuff? Fred making signs—ah, to put him up to it. I'll do so in Fred's own easy, elegant way!—You see, as Fred says, ceremonials and titles die in the youth of equality and the friendship of freedom!—No, that comes afterwards!—Prithee, dear Middlesex, where did you leave your cloak?

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: Middlesex again!—coupled, too, with such incongruous expressions; equality!—freedom!—My Lord Wilmot, permit me to request of your Lordship to order your people to convey to a distance, remote from my person,—that small man.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Small man!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: I enjoy this.

sp.speaker: WILMOT
sp.p: Make him apologise to the Duke,—then hurry him off into the next room. Allow me to explain to your Grace.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD
sp.p: But Fred himself—

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Fred himself is apologising. Mark how he bows and cringes,—bow and cringe, too.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: But what shall I say?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Anything most civil and servile.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: I—I—my Lord Duke, I really most humbly entreat your Grace's pardon, I—

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: Small man, your pardon is granted, for your existence is effaced. So far as my recognition is necessary to your sense of being, consider yourself henceforth—annihilated!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: I humbly thank your Grace! Annihilated! what's that?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Duke's English for excused.
sp.stage: (Softhead wants to get back to the Duke.)
sp.p: What! have not you had enough of the Duke?

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: No, now we've made it up. I never bear malice. I should like to know more of him; one can't get at a Duke every day. If he did call me “small man,” he is a Duke,—and such a remarkably fine one!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: You deserve to be haunted by him! No—no! Come into the next room and talk of your father. He carries a great many votes, and Sir Robert shall deal with him for cloth and for any other commodity he may desire to vend to the Premier.

div.stage: [Exeunt through side-door. Softhead very reluctant to leave the Duke.

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: There's something portentous in that small man's audacity. —Quite an aberration of Nature! Such things do happen in critical eras of the world, like the present.—Fie, my Lord, how can you associate with such a—very—small man! But we are alone now, we two gentlemen. Your father is my friend, and his son must have courage and honour.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Faith, I had the courage to say I would call your Grace “Middlesex,” and the honour to keep to my word. So I've given good proof that I've courage and honour enough for anything!

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: You're a wild boy. You have levities and follies. But alas! even rank does not exempt its possessor from the faults of humanity. Very strange! My own dead brother—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Your brother, Lord Henry de Mowbray? My dear Duke, pray forgive me; but I hope there's no truth in what Tonson, the bookseller, told me at Will's,—that your brother had left behind, certain Confessions or Memoirs, which are all that might be apprehended from a man of a temper so cynical, and whose success in the gay world was so—terrible.
Determined seducer and implacable cut-throat!)

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: Ha! then those Memoirs exist! My brother kept his profligate threat. I shall be ridiculed, lampooned. I, the head of the Mowbrays! Powers above, is nothing on earth, then, left sacred! My lord, I thank you sincerely. Can you learn in whose hands is this scandalous record?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: I will try. And I hope some honest man has got hold of it,—for Tonson told me he could not yet induce him to sell it. You would wish it supprest?

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: Supprest! In the bottomless pit!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: And would buy it yourself?

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: Myself! No. I would mortgage the Castle of Mowbray to save my name from the jests of a ribald,—that ribald, my kinsman! But to buy, myself, what was meant to expose me—, men would say the Duke of Middlesex feared—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Leave it to me. I know Lord Henry bore you a grudge for renouncing his connexion, on account of his faults—of humanity! His wit might not spare you; nor even what is more sacred,—the sex on which his life was one war. I remember an anecdote how he fought with a husband, some poor devil named Morland, for a boast in a tavern, which— Oh, but we'll not speak of that. We must get the Memoir. We gentlemen have all common cause here. Woman's name and man's hearth.

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: Worthy son of your father. You deserve, indeed, the trust that I come to confide to you. Drop this shameful digression. I have need of all my composure—you, of all your attention.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: What's coming, I wonder.

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: There is a Hanoverian gentleman of very good family, in his own country, but a perfect stranger to me—George Guelph. Certain persons who call themselves the People— but who, strange to say, did not do me the honour to ask my opinion—have placed this gentleman on the throne of our lawful sovereign, James the Third.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Hush, Duke, hush! This confidence is really so dangerous!

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: Dangerous, what one man of honour confides to another! Your interruption's unseemly. To proceed: his Majesty, King James, having been deceived by vague promises in the Expedition of 'Fifteen, has very properly refused to imperil his rights again, unless upon the positive pledge of a sufficient number of persons of influence, to risk life and all in his service. Myself and some others, not wholly unknown to you, propose to join in a pledge which our King with such reason exacts. Your assistance, my Lord, would be valuable, for you are the idol of the young. Doubts were entertained of your loyalty. I have come to dispel them—a word will suffice. If we succeed, you restore the son of a Stuart; if we fail, you will go to the scaffold by the side of John Duke of Middlesex! Can you hesitate; or, is silence assent?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Assent to surrender my country to the sword and the flames of civil war—for a cause that is hopeless!

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: Hopeless! But I cannot stoop to argue—'tis eno' for a man like me to invite. Does your Lordship refuse my invitation?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: My dear Duke, forgive me that I dismiss with a jest a subject so fatal, if gravely entertained. I have so many other engagements at present that, just to recollect them, I must keep my head on my shoulders. Accept my humblest excuses.

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: Accept mine for mistaking the son of Lord Loftus. I have the honour to wish your Lordship good day.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Lord Loftus again! Stay. Your Grace spoke of persons not wholly unknown to me. I entreat you to explain.

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: My Lord, I have trusted you with my own life; but to compromise by a word the life of another, permit me once more to repeat to your Lordship that I am John Duke of Middlesex.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Go thy ways for the most prejudiced piece of absurdity and bombast, valour and honour, that ever shook a plot from the curls of a periwig, or drew a court sword against the march of a nation. But can he allude to my father? Nay, scarcely; my father would surely have hinted to me if—still, I'm uneasy. How shall I find out?—Ha! Hardman. Hardman, I say! Here's a man who finds everything out.

Softhead, continue annihilated for the next five minutes or so. These books will help to the cessation of your existence mental and bodily. Mr. Locke, on the Understanding, will show that you have not an innate idea; and the Essay of Bishop Berkely will prove you have not an atom of matter.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: But—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: No buts!—they're the fashion.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Oh, if they're the fashion—

div.stage: [Seats himself at the further end of the room; commences vigorously with Berkely and Locke, first one and then the other, and after convincing himself that they are above his comprehension, gradually subsides from despair into dozing.

sp.speaker: WILMOT
sp.p: My dear Hardman, you are the only one of my friends, whom, in spite of your politics, my high Tory father condescends to approve of.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: Why, there are many sides to a character;

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: A favourite saying of mine, too;

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: And if I have a talent it is that of finding the right one.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Ah! talk to my poor father of me; and you are on his blind side in a moment.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: In truth, he has shown that I have his esteem; First, by asking me to lecture his son; Secondly, by forgiving the ill-success of the lectures.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Why, look you, this life! it is such a sunny, glorious, thing! It does so leap and sparkle in my veins that I cannot walk the thoroughfares of quiet men with their sober footstep. Yet, dear as existence, thus joyous, is, I would fling it from me as lightly as I toss this glove, to save that sober, preaching, father of mine from a single peril!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: I could almost love this man, if he would let me. Why do you so often belie yourself, by seeming worse than you are?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Why, don't you think that rogues who pretend to be honest, have had their day long eno'? and if we honest folks set up a counter hypocrisy, and pretend to be rogues, 'gad, we may drive the other fellows out of the fashion! But to come back to my father,—every one knows that his family were stout cavaliers, attached to the Stuarts.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Ah! I guess why the Jacobite Duke has been here. I must look up David Fallen; he is in all the schemes for the Stuarts.) Well—and—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
HARDMAN.
sp.p: Why not ask him yourself?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Alas! I'm in disgrace; he even begs me not to come to his house. You see he wants me to marry. Just like fathers! Ever since Agamemnon set them the bad example of sacrificing Iphigenia for a favourable breeze, they never think they've a chance of smooth sailing till they've bound us tight to the horns of the altar!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: But your father bade me tell you, he would leave your choice to yourself;—would marriage then seem so dreadful a sacrifice?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Sacrifice! Leave my choice to myself? My dear Father!
Smart!
Order my coach.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: This impatience looks very like love.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Pooh! what do you know about love?—you, who love only ambition! Solemn old jilt, with whom one's never safe from a rival.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Yes;—always safe from a rival both in love and ambition, if one will watch to detect, and then scheme to destroy him.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Destroy—ruthless exterminator! May we never be rivals! Pray keep to ambition.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: But ambition lures me to love. This fair Lucy Thornside, as rich as she's fair! Woe indeed to the man who shall be my rival with her. I will call there to-day.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Then, you'll see my father, and sound him?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: I will do so.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: You are the best friend I have. If ever I can serve you in return—

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Tut; in serving my friends, 'tis myself that I serve.

sp.speaker: WILMOT
sp.p: Pooh! there can be no danger. I've been hearing of plots ever since I was born, but nothing ever comes of them; and if I learn from Hardman that my father meditates the innocent amusement of blowing up the country—I'll turn steady myself and shame him out of such pranks! Now to Lucy. Ha! Softhead.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD
sp.p: Heh!

sp.speaker: WILMOT
sp.p: I must put this suspicious Sir Geoffrey on a wrong scent. If Softhead were to make love to the girl—violently— desperately.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD
sp.p: I would give the world to be tucked up in bed now!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: By Pluto and Hecate—the man's actually yawning!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Is there any harm in that?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: I've a project—an intrigue—be all life and all fire! Why, you tremble—

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: With excitement. Proceed!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: There's a certain snarling suspicious Sir Geoffrey Thornside, with a beautiful daughter, to whom he is a sort of a one-sided bear of a father—all growl and no hug.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: I know him!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: You. How?

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Why, his most intimate friend is Mr. Goodenough Easy.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Lucy presented me to a Mistress Barbara Easy. Pretty girl!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: You are not courting her?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Not at present. Are you?

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Why, my father wants me to marry her.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: They are all alike these fathers! That vile Agamemnon! You refused?

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: No. I did not.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Had she that impertinence?

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: No; but her father had. He wished for it once; but since I've become a man à-la-mode, and made a sensation at St. James's, he says that his daughter shall be courted no more by such a fine gentleman. Oh! he's low, Mr. Easy; very good-humoured and hearty, but respectable, sober, and square-toed;—decidedly low!—City bred! So I can't go much to his house; but I see Barbara sometimes at Sir Geoffrey's.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Excellent! Listen: I am bent upon adding Lucy Thornside to the list of my conquests.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: But—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: But how did I know her? I'll tell you. Between Hyde Park and Mayfair, there lie certain savage recesses, which in some distant age may be brought into fashion, but which now are frequented occasionally by snipes and habitually by footpads. About a week since, I chanced to be passing those desolate wilds when I heard female cries,—ran to the spot,—found two ruffians had stopped a sedan and dragged forth a young lady. Your stout heart conjectures the rest: —a blow to the one and a kick to the other, and I bear off the prettiest trembler that ever leant on the arm of knight-errant,—escorted her home,—called thrice since that fortunate hour, and my angel's name, among mortals, is Lucy Thornside.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: But I don't as yet see how I—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: You are so hot and impatient! Let me speak: her churl of a father has already given me to understand that he hates a lord—

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Hates a lord! Can such men be?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: And despises a man à la mode.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: I knew he was eccentric, but this is downright insanity.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Brief. I see very well that he'll soon shut his doors in my face, unless I make him believe that it is not his daughter who attracts me to his house; so I tell you what we will do; —You shall make love to Lucy—violent love, you rogue.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: But Sir Geoffrey knows I'm in love with the other.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: That's over. Father refused you—transfer of affection; natural pique and human inconstancy. And, in return, to oblige you, I'll make love just as violent to Mistress Barbara Easy.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Stop, stop; I don't see the necessity of that.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Pooh! nothing more clear. Having thus duped the two lookers on, we shall have ample opportunity to change partners, and hands across, then down the middle and up again.

sp.speaker: SMART.
sp.p: Your coach waits, my Lord.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Come along. Fie! that's not the way to conduct a cane. Has not Mr. Pope, our great poet of fashion, given you the nicest instructions in that art?“Sir Plume, of amber snuff-box justly vain, And the nice conduct of a clouded cane.” The cane does not conduct you; you conduct the cane. Thus, with a debonnair swing. Now, t'other hand on your haunch; easy, dégagé—impudently graceful; with the air of a gentleman, and the heart of a—monster! Allons! Vive la joie.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Vive la jaw, indeed. I feel as if I were going to be hanged. Allons! Vive la jaw!

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: [Library in the House of Sir Geoffrey Thornside.—At the back a large Window opening nearly to the ground.—Side-door to an adjoining room.—Style of decoration, that introduced from the Dutch in the reign of William III. (old-fashioned, therefore, at the date assigned to the Play)—rich and heavy; oak pannels, partly gilt; high-backed chairs, &c.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: But, I say, the dog did howl last night, and it is a most suspicious circumstance.

sp.speaker: HODGE.
sp.p: Fegs, my dear Measter, if you'se think that these Lunnon thieves have found out that your honour's rents were paid last woik, mayhap I'd best sleep here in the loibery.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: How does he know I keep my monies here?

sp.speaker: HODGE.
sp.p: Zooks! I 'se the old blunderbuss, and that will boite better than any dog, I'se warrant!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: I begin to suspect him. For ten years have I nursed that viper at my hearth, and now he wants to sleep in my library, with a loaded blunderbuss, in case I should come in and detect him. I see murder in his very face. How blind I've been!) Hodge, you are very good—very; come closer.—
What a felon step he has!) But I don't keep my rents here, they're all gone to the banker's.

sp.speaker: HODGE.
sp.p: Mayhap I'd best go and lock up the pleate; or will you send that to the banker's?

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: I wonder if he has got an accomplice at the banker's! it looks uncommonly like it.) No, I'll not send the plate to the banker's, I'll—consider. You've not detected the miscreant who has been flinging flowers into the library the last four days?

sp.speaker: HODGE.
sp.p: Noa, Sir Geoffrey; I'se got 'em all safe in the coal-hole! —but there beant any gunpowder in 'em. What your honour took for the head of an adder was—a sweet-pea!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Ugh!—just like servants! If they saw their master in the folds of a boa constrictor, they'd tell him it was a climbing honeysuckle.) Well, and of course you've not observed any one watching your master, when he walks in his garden, from the window of that ugly old house in Deadman's Lane?

sp.speaker: HODGE.
sp.p: With the sign of the Crown and Poor-Culley! Why, it maun be very leately. 'Tint a week ago sin' it war empty.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: How he evades the question!—just as they do at the Old Bailey.) Get along with you, and feed the house-dog —he's honest!

sp.speaker: HODGE.
sp.p: Yes, your honour.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: How eagerly he said “Yes”—very suspicious. Perhaps he wants to poison the dog—not a doubt of it. Hodge!— Hodge!—
Don't feed the dog; I'll feed him myself.

sp.speaker: HODGE.
sp.p: Yes, your honour.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: I'm a very unhappy man, very! Never did harm to any one—done good to many. And ever since I was a babe in the cradle, all the world have been conspiring and plotting against me. It certainly is an exceedingly wicked world; and what its attraction can be to the other worlds, that they should have kept it spinning through space for six thousand years, I can't possibly conceive—unless they are as bad as itself; I should not wonder. That new theory of attraction is a very suspicious circumstance against the planets—there's a gang of 'em!
sp.stage: (A bunch of flowers is thrown in at the window.)
sp.p: Heaven defend me! There it is again! This is the fifth bunch of flowers that's been thrown at me through the window—what can it possibly mean?—the most alarming circumstance!
sp.stage: (Cautiously poking at the flowers with his sword.)

sp.speaker: MR. GOODENOUGH EASY
sp.p: Yes, Barbara, go and find Mistress Lucy. Never mind announcing me, Hodge, I'm at home here.
How d'ye do, my hearty?

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Ugh! hearty, indeed!

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Why, what's the matter? what are you poking at those flowers for; is there a snake in them?

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Worse than that, I suspect! Hem! Goodenough Easy, I believe I may trust you—

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: You trusted me once with five thousand pounds.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Dear, dear, I forgot that. But you paid me back, Easy?

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Of course; but the loan saved my credit, and made my fortune: so the favour's the same.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Ugh! Don't say that; favours and perfidy go together! a truth I learned early in life. What favours I heaped on my foster-brother! And did not he conspire with my cousin to set my own father against me; and trick me out of my heritage?

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: But you've heaped favours as great on the son of that scamp of a foster-brother; and he—

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Ay! but he don't know of them. And then there was my —that girl's mother—

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Ah! that was an affliction which might well turn a man pre-inclined to suspicion, into a thorough self-tormenter for the rest of his life. But she loved you dearly once, old friend; and were she yet alive, and could be proved guiltless after all—

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Guiltless! Sir—?

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Well—well! we agreed never to talk upon that subject. Come, come, what of the nosegay?

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Yes, yes, the nosegay! Hark! I suspect some design on my life. The dog howled last night. When I walk in the garden, somebody or something (can't see what it is) seems at the watch in a window in Deadman's Lane—pleasant name for a street at the back of one's premises! And what looks blacker than all, for five days running, has been thrown in at me, yonder, surreptitiously and anonymously, what you call—a nosegay!

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Ha! ha! you lucky dog!—you are still not bad-looking! Depend on it, the flowers come from a woman.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: A woman!—my worst fears are confirmed! In the small city of Placentia, in one year, there were no less than seven hundred cases of slow poisoning, and all by women. Flowers were among the instruments they employed, steeped in laurel-water and other mephitic preparations. Those flowers are poisoned. Not a doubt of it!—how very awful!

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: But why should any one take the trouble to poison you, Geoffrey?

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: I don't know. But I don't know why seven hundred people in one year were poisoned in Placentia. Hodge! Hodge!
Bring a shovel and brush!—sweep away those flowers!— lock 'em up with the rest in the coal-hole. I'll examine them all chemically, by and by, with precaution.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: But, Geoffrey, when a man has a daughter of an age in which flowers are not locked up in a coal-hole, mayn't he suspect that such mephitic preparations are intended for her?

div.stage: Enter Hodge to remove the flowers.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Ugh!—as if I had not thought that at first; but why should they always be thrown into my special sitting-room, at the very hour I enter it, only when I'm alone?
Don't smell at 'em; and, above all, don't let the house-dog smell at 'em.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Ha! ha!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Ugh!—that brute's laughing!—no more feeling than a brickbat!) Goodenough Easy; you are a very happy man.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Happy, yes. I could be happy on bread and water!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: And would toast your bread at a conflagration, and fill your jug from a deluge! Ugh! I've a trouble you are more likely to feel for, as you've a girl of your own to keep out of mischief. A man named Wilmot, and styled “my Lord,” has called here three times; he pretends he saved my— ahem!—that is Lucy, from footpads, when she was coming home from your house in a sedan chair. And I suspect that the man means to make love to her!—

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Egad! that's the only likely suspicion you've hit on this many a day. I've heard of Lord Wilmot. Softhead professes to copy him. Rather a madcap. But his companions adore him. Wish you joy!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Joy!—you have the strangest expressions!—there's no wringing sympathy out of you. Joy, indeed! a gay man à la mode! I've seen eno' of such villains. No girl whom I can control shall ever marry one of those heroes of Congreve and Wycherley. Ugh! you did right, for once in your life, when you broke off the match between Mr. Softhead and Barbara, on the ground that the fool had become—a fine gentleman!

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: O Lord, just the reverse!—that the fool could never become a fine gentleman! I'm not severe; but I am independent. If there's a thing I despise in the world, 'tis a simpleton led away by example. Every class has its faults and its merits. Let each stick to its own. Softhead, the son of a trader! he be a lounger at White's and Will's, and dine with wits and fine gentlemen! He live with lords!—he mimic fashion! No! I've respect for even the faults of a man; but I've none for the tricks of a monkey.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Ugh! you're so savage on Softhead, I suspect 'tis from envy. Man and monkey, indeed! If a ribbon is tied to the tail of a monkey, it is not the man it enrages; it is some other monkey whose tail has no ribbon!

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: I disdain your insinuations. Do you mean to imply that I am a monkey? I won't praise myself; but at least a more steady, respectable, sober—

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Ugh! sober!—I suspect you'd get as drunk as a lord, if a lord passed the bottle.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Now, now, now. Take care;—you'll put me in a passion.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: There—there—beg pardon. But I fear you've a sneaking respect for a lord—

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Sir, I respect the British Constitution and the House of Peers as a part of it; but as for a lord in himself, with a mere handle to his name, a paltry title! That can have no effect on a Briton, of independence and sense. And that's just the difference between Softhead and me. But as you don't like for a son-in-law, the real fine gentleman; perhaps you've a mind to the copy. I am sure you are welcome to Softhead.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Ugh! I've other designs for the girl.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Have you? What? Perhaps your favourite, young Hardman?—by the way, I've not met him here lately.

sp.speaker: LUCY.
sp.p: O, my dear father, forgive me if I disturb you; but I did so long to see you!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: LUCY.
sp.p: Because Hodge told me you'd been alarmed last night— the dog howled! But it was full moon last night, and he will howl at the moon!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: How did she know it was full moon? I suspect she was looking out of the window—

div.stage: Enter Hodge announcing Lord Wilmot and Mr. Shadowly Softhead.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Wilmot! my suspicions are confirmed; she was looking out of the window! This comes of Shakspeare having written that infernal incendiary trash about Romeo and Juliet!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Your servant, ladies;—Sir Geoffrey, your servant. I could not refuse Mr. Softhead's request to inquire after your health.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: I thank your lordship; but when my health wants inquiring after, I send for the doctor.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Is it possible you can do anything so dangerous and rash?

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: How?—how?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Send for the very man who has an interest in your being ill!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: That's very true. I did not think he had so much sense in him!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: I need not inquire how you are, ladies? When Hebé retired from the world, she divided her bloom between you. Mistress Barbara, vouchsafe me the honour a queen accords to the meanest of her gentlemen.

div.stage: [Kisses Barbara's hand, and leads her aside, conversing in dumb show.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Ah, Mistress Lucy, vouchsafe me the honour which—But she don't hold her hand in the same position.

sp.speaker: LUCY.
sp.p: What did you say, Mr. Softhead?

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Hem! How was it?—oh, the meanest of your majesty's gentlemen.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Bravo!—bravo! Master Softhead!—Encore!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Bravo!—Encore! I don't understand you, Mr. Easy.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: That bow of yours! Perfect! Plain to see you have not forgotten the old Dancing Master in Crooked Lane.

sp.speaker: LUCY.
sp.p: Fie, Mr. Easy!—your bow's charming, Mr. Shadowly.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: It is not a common bow, I confess; I and Lord Wilmot— that is my friend, Fred, yonder, have a bow of our own. We are so alike in all things. We are often mistaken for each other—
—I'm not an inconstant man; but I'll show that City fellow, there are other ladies in town besides his daughter)—Dimidum meæ, how pretty you are, Mistress Lucy!

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Ha! ha! Geoffrey, I said you were welcome to Softhead. Quick work. One would think he'd overheard, and was taking me at my word.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: And I see that popinjay of a lord is more attentive to Barbara than ever he was to the other.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Hey! hey! D'ye think so?

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: I suspect he has heard how rich you are. He seems a brisk, lively rogue. Best look sharp,—just one of those Hymen-men, who knock down a father before he knows where he is, with ‘Stand and deliver! your child and your money!’

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Certainly I should scorn to ask a lord to marry my daughter; but if he were to ask me—'Pon my life, I think there's something in it.

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: Papa, Lord Wilmot begs to be presented to you.

div.stage: [Bows interchanged. Wilmot offers snuff-box. Easy at first declines, then accepts—sneezes violently; unused to snuff.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: He! he! quite clear!—titled fortune-hunter. Over head and ears in debt, I dare say. Found out from poor Softhead that Easy's as rich as a Jew; and now the mercenary wretch is trying to supplant his own friend. If so, Lucy's safe! Nobody knows how rich I am—take very good care of that. But I'll make all sure.
Pretty girl, Mistress Barbara! Eh?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Pretty! Say beautiful!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: He! he! Her father will give her fifty thousand pounds down on the wedding day. Better off than my girl, who (if she marry with my consent) would only have a poor little property of the worst land in Norfolk, and not a rood of that till I'm dead. And, zounds my lord! I'm vigorous, and intend to live these thirty years.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: The paternal enemy falls into the ambush.) Fifty thousand pounds on the wedding day! She's the loveliest creature I ever saw!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Tho' her father's in commerce, you fine gentlemen don't live as if you had much respect for your ancestors: you are too liberal to think that a man's want of birth should prevent him from satisfying your want of money.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Indeed I am, and I venerate the British merchant who can give his daughter fifty thousand pounds! What a smile she has!
I say, Sir Geoffrey, you see I'm very shy—bashful indeed—and Mr. Easy is watching every word I say to his daughter: so embarrassing! Could'nt you get him out of the room?

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Mighty bashful indeed! Turn the oldest friend I have out of my room, in order that you may make love to his daughter!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: I say, Mr. Easy. My double there, Softhead, is so shy— bashful indeed—and that suspicious Sir Geoffrey is watching every word he says to Mistress Lucy: so embarrassing! Do get your friend out of the room, will you?

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Ha! ha! Certainly, my Lord.

I see he wants to be alone with my Barbara. What will they say in Lombard-street when she's my Lady? Shouldn't wonder if they returned me M.P. for the City). Come into the next room, Geoffrey; and tell me your designs for Lucy.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Oh, very well! You wish to encourage that pampered young—Satrap! How he does love a lord, and how a lord does love 50,000l.! He! he! I know a little of the world. He! he!

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Monstrous fine young man that, Mistress Lucy,—not a bit proud—no airs and graces.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Oh, the best little fellow in the world, my friend Fred—

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Your friend Fred! Mr. Softhead, I despise the man who has his head so turned by a lord.

sp.speaker: WILMOT
sp.stage: (running to LUCY, and pushing aside SOFTHEAD).
sp.p: Return to your native allegiance. Truce with the enemy, and exchange of prisoners.

div.stage: [Leads Lucy aside—She rather grave and reluctant.

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: So, you'll not speak to me, Mr. Softhead; words are too rare with you fine gentlemen, to throw away upon old friends.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Ahem!

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: You don't remember the winter evenings you used to pass at our fireside? nor the mistletoe bough at Christmas? nor the pleasant games at Blind-man's Buff and Hunt the Slipper? nor the strong tea I made you when you had the migraine? nor how I prevented your eating Banbury cake at supper, when you know it always disagrees with you?— But, I suppose you are so hardened that you can eat Banbury cake every night, now!—I'm sure it is nothing to me!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Those recollections of one's early innocence are very melting! One renounces a great deal of happiness for renown and ambition.—Barbara!

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: Shadowly!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: However one may rise in life,—however the fashion may compel one to be a monster—

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: A monster!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Yes, Fred and I are both monsters! Still—still—still— 'Ecod, I do love you with all my heart, and that's the truth of it.

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: Oh, Shadowly! that dear Lord Wilmot!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD
sp.stage: (alarmed and clapping his hand to his sword).
sp.p: Ha! the villain!

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: He says he's sure you've never been false.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Fred's a jewel! what a pity your Cit of a father can't abide the upper walks of society.

sp.speaker: LUCY.
sp.p: Nay, my Lord, this looks so like deceit!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: But you must pardon a deceit that's so harmless. Sir Geoffrey's prejudice against me must be humoured till I've time to remove it. I cannot live without seeing you—you have bewitched me!

sp.speaker: LUCY.
sp.p: Ah—my Lord! I'm afraid you've been very often— bewitched!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Fie! you are as suspicious as your father.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Your Lordship's reputation is far beyond—suspicions

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: She's been inquiring into my reputation. An excellent symptom! But, my charming Lucy—when one takes up the character of a servant, 'tis a sort of etiquette to engage him.

sp.speaker: LUCY.
sp.p: Surely that depends on the character?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: And what can be said against mine?

sp.speaker: LUCY.
sp.p: Only that your Lordship is not—a very faithful servant!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Her archness delights me. I have found what I have sought all my life, the union of spirit and sweetness, innocence and gaiety. Oh, Lucy, if the renunciation of all youthful levities and follies, if the most steadfast adherence to your side—despite all the chances of life, all temptations, all dangers—

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: Hist! some one coming.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Change partners; hands across. My angel Barbara!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Lord Wilmot here!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: What! does he know Sir Geoffrey?

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: Oh yes. Sir Geoffrey thinks there's nobody like him.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Footpads! Hum! And pray how long since?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Well met, my dear Hardman. So you are intimate here?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Ay; and you?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: An acquaintance in its cradle; just a week old. Droll man, Sir Geoffrey; I delight in odd characters. Besides, here are other attractions.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: If he be my rival! Hum! I hear from David Fallen that his father's on the brink of high treason! That secret gives a hold on the son.

sp.speaker: WILMOT
sp.p: You understand; 'tis a compact. You will favour my stratagem?

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: Yes,; and you'll engage to cure Softhead of his taste for the fashion, and send him back to—the City.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Since you live in the City, and condescend to regard such a monster!

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: Why, we were brought up together. His health is so delicate; I should like to take care of him.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: If that is not woman all over, I don't know what is!

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: And he's not so bad as he seems. Heigho! I am afraid 'tis too late, and papa will never forgive his past follies.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Yet papa seems very good-natured. Perhaps there's another side to his character?

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: Oh yes! He is such a very independent man, my papa! and has such a contempt for people who go out of their own rank, and make fools of themselves for the sake of example.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Never fear; I'll ask him to dine, and open his heart with a cheerful glass.

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: Cheerful glass! You don't know papa—the soberest man! If there's any thing on which he's severe, 'tis a cheerful glass.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: So, so! Does not he ever—get a little excited?

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: Excited! Don't think of it! Besides, he is so in awe of Sir Geoffrey, who would tease him out of his life, if he could but hear that papa was so inconsistent as to—as to—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: As to get—a little excited?

These hints should suffice me! 'Gad, if I could make him tipsey for once in a way!—I'll try.) Adieu, my sweet Barbara, and rely on the zeal of your faithful ally. Stay; tell Mr. Easy that he must lounge into Will's. I will look out for him there in about a couple of hours. He'll meet many friends from the City, and all the wits and fine gentlemen. Don't forget.

Yes, I shall find Tonson at Will's. Let me see. Set Hardman to keep my wise father from mischief;—get at that diabolical Memoir;—intoxicate Easy;—cure Softhead of Fashion;—call to-night on the Lady of Mystery, Deadman's Lane;—meanwhile stole a march on General “Ugh! I suspect;”—and half-way to a wife! 'Gad, 'tis not such a dull day after all!) Allons! Vive la joie! Softhead, we'll have a night of it!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Ah! those were pleasant nights when one went to bed at half after ten. Heigho! Adieu, Barbara.

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: Adieu, Shadowly.

sp.speaker: LUCY.
sp.p: Where are you going, dear?

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: Just into the garden, to have a good cry. I'll be back presently.

div.stage: [Exit. Lucy takes her work, and sits.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Hum! I'm perplexed. Can it be Barbara? Yet Lucy looks changed since I saw her last—since Wilmot has known her—more grave. I dread to—

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Ah, Mr. Hardman!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Why that sigh? You, sad, whose happy mirth—

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Is not always sincere. Ah, Mr. Hardman, my father confides to you many of his secrets. Did he ever tell you what fault I can amend, so that he might love me better? Not once from my cradle has he even called me by the sweet name of child.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Nay, 'tis but his humours that conceal from you his heart. A parent's love is too precious a thing to be doubted lightly. But perhaps it is a mother that you miss?

sp.speaker: LUCY.
sp.p: I never remember to have seen one; but I miss her daily.
And never more than now!)

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Be comforted. My lot is harder than yours. Far as I can look back into childhood—motherless, fatherless, homeless, friendless, lonely—

sp.speaker: LUCY.
sp.p: Poor Mr. Hardman. I did not dream that you had such cause for sorrow. Seeing you so occupied and ambitious, one would not guess you concealed feelings thus deep.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: What! are deep feelings the monopoly of triflers? Does the heart only beat under the velvet and laces of those spoiled darlings of fortune?

sp.speaker: LUCY.
sp.p: What spoiled darlings of fortune?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Men like the sleek lord whom I found here! Men who are born to the hill top that we sons of labour reach but to die. Ah, were the world but a stage, they might have their first choice of the pageant and wardrobe; I would grudge not the spangles and tinsel.

sp.speaker: LUCY.
sp.p: Dear Mr. Hardman; you—
I never saw him so before!)

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: But the world's something more than a stage. Man is not always an actor. And woe to those darlings of fortune, when in the great war of the passions they strive, breast to breast, with us, stern sons of labour! They, unnerved by the sunshine,—we, braced by the storm. Ha! Ha!—we are stronger than they!

sp.speaker: LUCY.
sp.p: You are strangely moved, Mr. Hardman. Have you any quarrel with him—with Lord Wilmot?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: I betray myself like an infant.) Lord Wilmot! 'Twas an old, very old, but very sore recollection of very different persons—mere triflers—that made me unjust for a moment—to a man of the rarest accomplishments. Pray, what do you think of Lord Wilmot?

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.stage: (resuming her work with her face turned away).
sp.p: Indeed I can't say; I have seen him so seldom.

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: I think him—

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: You! yes, you think him?—

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: The most charming, irresistible—heigho!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Indeed! he seemed most attentive to you. Now I look at the girl, she's not ugly. I trust that the feeling's reciprocal?

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: It ought to be—if there's any believing the promises and vows of you dangerous, deceitful men.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Promises—vows! Now I look again, the girl's pretty— decidedly pretty! exceedingly pretty! Why not she, after all?

sp.speaker: BARBARA
sp.p: Do you think a poor innocent girl may safely trust her heart to Lord Wilmot?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Indeed I do; the most honourable of men!

Even were it so, dare I hope for myself? So fair, and an heiress! Tut! Have I ever yet failed in my struggle through life, aided but by my will and my brain? And now this two-fold prize. Love for my happiness— wealth for my ambition. Scheme now, plotting brain,— dare now, stubborn will!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: There he is—seated apart—will not even speak to that girl in my absence. So punctiliously honourable!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: But the father's consent! Bah! I've already got at the right side of his character.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Hush! Muttering some speech in defence of his country.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: If, too, I could get that place in the Treasury!—Make my suit less presumptuous. Shall I write to Sir Robert?—

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY
sp.p: He! he! my dear Hardman. We guess your thoughts.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Heh! Sir Geoffrey, you startle me.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Hope it will succeed.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: What succeed?

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Pooh! don't look so embarrassed and awkward. I'm a bit of an orator myself, and we all know that young members get their speeches by heart.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Oh! you are so shrewd, Mr. Easy.

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: Not I; but you do know everything. Intimate with Lord Wilmot, eh? Fine young man! Smitten with my little girl! But that suspicious old snarler says, 'tis all for her money. Should not like that. My Lord's not in debt, eh?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Debt! he abhors it. Generous; but prudent. I know all his affairs.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY
sp.p: He! he! I did it. Said she'd fifty thousand pounds.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: You are the most sagacious, incomparable man!
I am assured! Wilmot is not my rival. I'll save his father. David Fallen meets Lord Loftus at Will's. I'll be there.) My dear Sir Geoffrey!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: I'm not like Easy. I have a pedigree, as long as a Welchman's—much good it ever did me! I'd rather give my heiress to a man who made his own way through life than to a—

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: You would?
I will write to Walpole at once for that place.) Bless me, how late it is! I must be off. Goodbye, Mr. Easy. My heartfelt congratulations. I shall be at Will's myself—later. Good-bye, Sir Geoffrey.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Ugh! always in a hurry.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: But always getting on. What's your secret?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: This. The way to get on is to be never behind time. More than that, Mr. Easy—what is mind without action? a watch without hands!—the wheels may go round, the chainwork may lengthen—what use in either unless the hands make us sure of the moment and hour? Wheel and hands—thought and action—brain and will. Your hand, Mistress Lucy!

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Quite the man of business! So—what I call—practical! Very clever fellow!

sp.speaker: BARBARA
sp.stage: (aside to LUCY, her finger on her lip).
sp.p: Yet, I think I have puzzled him.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: I am sure he himself is a puzzle.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Ugh! as honest as Truth—

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: And as deep as her well!

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: Will's Coffee-house; occupying the depth of the stage. Various groups; Lord le Trimmer, Sir Thomas Timid, Colonel Flint, Jacob Tonson, &c; some seated in boxes, some standing. In a box at the side, David Fallen seated, writing. Enter Easy.

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.stage: (speaking to various acquaintances as he passes to the background).
sp.p: How d'ye do?—Have you seen my Lord Wilmot?—Good day.—Yes; I seldom come here; but I've promised to meet an intimate friend of mine—Lord Wilmot.—Servant, sir!— looking for my friend Wilmot:—Oh! not come yet!—hum —ha!—Charming young man, Wilmot:—head of the mode; generous, but prudent. I know all his affairs.
Great news! great news! Suspected Jacobite Plot!— Fears of ministers!—Army to be increased! Great news!

div.stage: [Coffee-house frequenters gather round Newsman—take papers— form themselves into fresh groups. Enter Hardman.

sp.speaker: SEVERAL VOICES.
sp.p: There's Hardman—the rising Member of Parliament— hand in glove with Sir Robert!—knows everything!

div.stage: [Crowd round Hardman, and seem to question him in dumb show.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Ha! ha!—Sir Robert Walpole alarmed? Never saw him in such spirits. Oh, sir, must not believe any newspaper except the ministerial!—Funds fallen, you say?—Well, I should not let out state secrets; but this I will tell you in confidence—keep in Sir Robert, and the Funds will be up ten per cent. in a fortnight.

My dear lord, you 're the very man I want to see. The Lieutenancy for your county is just vacant. In these critical times, who but your lordship should have that office? Go and call on Sir Robert. He only wants that attention to make you the offer.

sp.speaker: LORD LE TRIMMER.
sp.p: Me! But I don't quite agree with—

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Make haste; or your neighbour, Lord Graspall, will be there before you.

sp.speaker: LORD LE TRIMMER.
sp.p: Graspall should not have it, if I went on my knees for it. A thousand thanks to you, Mr. Hardman.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Secured a waverer.
Sir Thomas, a word with you. I am a plain man, and I love you. There's a conspiracy afloat; your name is suspected. There's been talk of the Tower.

sp.speaker: SIR THOMAS.
sp.p: Suspected! The Tower! What am I to do?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Vote with ministers for increasing the army, and you are safe.

sp.speaker: SIR THOMAS.
sp.p: Why, as to increasing the army—

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: When a man is suspected by the Government, there is but one course to pursue. For that Government he must vote thick and thin.

sp.speaker: SIR THOMAS.
sp.p: I'm eternally obliged to you, Mr. Hardman. The Tower! What an escape I have had?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: You may just give a hint to your friends.
Frightened a conspirator, and fright is contagious. Hit them both on the right side of the character.

I serve Walpole well. The means may be doubtful; I'm content with the end. For at heart I love England and freedom, and Walpole steers both through Charybdis and Scylla—civil war and the Stuart. I have sent off my letter; this place,—he must give it; the first favour I have asked. Hope smiles; I am at peace with all men. Now to save Wilmot's father.
sp.stage: (Approaches the box at which David Fallen is writing, and stoops down, as if arranging his buckle.)
sp.p: Hist! Whatever the secret, remember, not a word save to me)

div.stage: [Passes down the stage, and is eagerly greeted by various frequenters of the Coffee-house.

sp.speaker: LORD LOFTUS.
sp.p: Drawer, I engage this box; give me the newspaper. So— ‘Rumoured Jacobite plot—’

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: My dear lord, I obey your appointment. But is not the place you select rather strange?

sp.speaker: LOFTUS.
sp.p: Be seated, I pray you. No place so fit for our purpose. First, because its very publicity prevents all suspicion. We come to a coffee-house, where all ranks and all parties assemble, to hear the news, like the rest. And, secondly, we could scarcely meet our agent anywhere else. He is a Tory pamphleteer; was imprisoned for our sake in the time of William and Mary. If we, so well known to be Tories, are seen to confer with him here, 'twill only be thought that we are suggesting some points in a pamphlet. But you have read the papers; a plot is suspected. You are sure that King James is a Protestant?

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: Assured of it. I could not serve him if he were not. My ancestors took part in the Reformation.

sp.speaker: LORD LOFTUS.
sp.p: The army's to be increased.

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: Let a thing called a Government levy its hirelings; the true force of the country is with the Barons of England. We proved that—in the days of King John.

sp.speaker: LOFTUS
sp.p: That's a long time ago! 'Tis my honour I obey, not my reason. Thank heaven, in affecting to banish my Frederic from my house, I have kept him clear from even a suspicion that may attach to myself. My gallant, joyous son! May I beckon our agent?

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: Certainly. He risks his life for us; he shall be duly rewarded. Let him sit by our side.

div.stage: [LORD LOFTUS motions to David Fallen, who takes up his pamphlet and approaches openly.

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: I have certainly seen somewhere before that very thin man. Be seated, sir. Honourable danger makes all men equal.

sp.speaker: FALLEN.
sp.p: No, my Lord Duke. I know you not. It is the Earl I confer with.
I never stood in his hall, with lackeys and porters.)

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: Powers above! That scare-crow rejects my acquaintance! —Portentous!

sp.speaker: LOFTUS.
sp.p: Observe, Duke, we speak in a sort of jargon. Pamphlet means messenger.
Well, Mr. Fallen, when will the pamphlet be ready?

sp.speaker: FALLEN
sp.p: Tomorrow, my Lord, exactly at one o'clock.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: I don't understand—

sp.speaker: LOFTUS.
sp.p: Hush! Walpole laughs at pamphlets, but would hang messengers.
To-morrow, not to-day? Well, more time for—

sp.speaker: FALLEN.
sp.p: Subscribers. Thank you, my Lord.
Where shall the messenger meet you?

sp.speaker: LOFTUS.
sp.p: At the back of the Duke's new house in Bond Street, there is a quiet, lone place—

sp.speaker: FALLEN
sp.p: By the wall of Lord Berkely's garden? I know it. The messenger shall be there. The signal word, ‘Marston Moor.’ No conversation should pass. But who brings the packet? That's the first step of danger.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Then 'tis mine, sir, in right of my birth.

sp.speaker: FALLEN
sp.p: I'll attend to all your lordship's suggestions; they're excellent, and will startle this vile administration. Many thanks to your lordship.

div.stage: [Returns to his table and resumes his writing. Groups point and murmur. Jacob Tonson advances.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: That pestilent scribbler, David Fallen! Another libellous pamphlet as bitter as the last, I'll swear.

sp.speaker: TONSON.
sp.p: Bitter as gall, sir, I am proud to say. Your servant; Jacob Tonson, the bookseller,—at your service. I advanced a pound upon it.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: I really wonder Walpole does not prosecute.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Prosecute? He would rather pay for it. 'Tis his maxim, that one scurrilous pamphlet saves a country from fifty conspiracies. You look surprised, gentlemen: why, I remember, three months ago, when our friend Mr. Easy here was teased with the nettle-rash, that his doctor said— ‘Don't complain, Mr. Easy, a strong constitution throws out an eruption; a weak one would have smouldered away in a fever.’ Disaffection when printed is only a nettle-rash, and the life of nations is saved when disease is thrown out on the surface.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: He knows I had the nettle-rash! Wonderful man, knows everything!

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: I will meet you in the Mall to-morrow, a quarter after one precisely. We may go now? Powers above—his mind's distracted—he walks out before me!

sp.speaker: LOFTUS
sp.p: I follow you, Duke.

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: My dear friend—if you really insist on it?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Mr. Easy, I'll bet you ten guineas I find out what those Tories told David Fallen to put in his pamphlet.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Well, you are certain to win, but I can afford to lose; and I should like to know. Done!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Drawer, a bottle of Claret—at this table.

div.stage: [Bows to Fallen and sits down; Fallen scowling at him.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: What a clever imperturbable dog it is—so thoroughly practical! Finds out everything, that Hardman! Sure to rise, eh!

div.stage: [Coffee-house frequenters evince their admiration and assent.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.stage: (as the Drawer places the wine, &c. on the table.)
sp.p: Let me offer you a glass of wine, Mr. Fallen—
Well?—

div.stage: [Fallen, who has been writing, pushes the paper towards him.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: “At one to-morrow—the wall by Lord Berkely's—Marston Moor—The Duke in person”—So! We must save these men. I will call on you in the morning, and concert the means.

sp.speaker: FALLEN.
sp.p: Yes, save, not destroy, these enthusiasts. I'm resigned to the name of a hireling—not to that of a butcher!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: You serve both Whig and Jacobite; do you care then for either?

sp.speaker: FALLEN.
sp.p: Sneering politician! what has either cared for me? I entered the world, devoted heart and soul to two causes—the throne of the Stuart, the glory of Letters. I saw them both as a poet. My father left me no heritage but loyalty and learning. He sold all he had to levy troops for King Charles, and buried his gold in the red field of Marston Moor. Charles the Second praised my verse, and I starved: James the Second praised my prose, and I starved; the reign of King William—I passed that in prison!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: But the ministers of Anne were gracious to writers.

sp.speaker: FALLEN.
sp.p: And offered me a pension to belie my past life, and write Odes on the Queen who had dethroned her own father. I was not then disenchanted—I refused. That's years ago. If I starved, I had fame. Now came my worst foes, my own fellow-writers. What is fame but a fashion? A jest upon Grub Street, a rhyme from young Pope, could jeer a score of grey labourers like me out of their last consolation. Time and hunger tame all. I could still starve myself; I have six children at home—they must live.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: This man has genius—he might have been a grace to his age. I'm perplexed; Sir Robert—

sp.speaker: FALLEN.
sp.p: Disdains Letters—I've renounced them. He pays services like these. Well—I serve him. Leave me; go!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: Not so bad as he seems—another side to the character: this moves me; I've been a writer myself. But the remedy? A state may but humble by alms; a minister corrupt by a bribe: what Patron then for Letters!—The public?—yes, for the Author, whose talents the Public may chance to appreciate. And for those who, with toils as severe, but with genius less shaped to the taste of the many, can win not the ear of the day, why perhaps in some far distant age, when eno' of the strong have dropped to death broken-hearted, and eno' of the weak (bowed down by the tyrant Necessity,) have veiled in shame and despair the eyes that once looked to the stars; these rival children of light may learn at last, that the tie they now rend should be the bond to unite them, and help one another. I have lost the bet, Mr. Easy.

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: Hardman's not so clever as I thought he was, by ten guineas.

div.stage: [Coffee-house frequenters evince their assent, but no longer their admiration.
Enter Drawer, with a letter to Hardman.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: From Walpole! Now then! my fate—my love—my fortunes!

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: He has got a letter from the Prime Minister, marked ‘private and confidential.”
After all, he is a very clever fellow.

div.stage: [Coffee-house frequenters evince the readiest assent, and the liveliest admiration.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: “My dear Hardman,—Extremely sorry; in these times Government must strengthen itself amongst the doubtful. Place in question absolutely wanted to conciliate some noble family otherwise dangerous. Another time, more fortunate. Fully sensible of your valuable services.—Robert Walpole.” —Refused! Let him look to himself! I will—I will—Alas! he is needed by my country; and I am powerless against him.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Drawer! a private room—covers for six—dinner in an hour! And—drawer! Tell Mr. Tonson not to go yet. Softhead, we'll have an orgy to-night, worthy the days of King Charles the Second. What's your favourite wine?

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: For Heaven's sake, not that diabolical Burgundy!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Disloyal to Burgundy! the only wine now in fashion,— unless, by the bye, you prefer aqua-fortis? Drawer!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: No—no—no! Let it be Burgundy! Homicide!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Just as you like. Let me see—there'll be six of us—a dozen to each. Drawer,—send to Lockett's for six dozen of Burgundy—other wines in proportion. By the way, Softhead, you smoke, of course?

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Smoke! that filthy tobacco! Not I. Tried it once at the Twopenny Club, and felt as if on board ship, with the sea rolling mountains! The beastliest thing—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Not smoke, and pretend to be a man à la mode?

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Come, come, that's too good! All the fishwomen in Billingsgate smoke—seen them myself, and heard them, too— railing, abusive, impudent creatures!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Of course, they are. The impudence of Billingsgate gives the mode to St. James's! only here, names are different. There abuse, and here scandal. There railing,—here wit.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: As for wit, I'm a match for the best of you!—but tobacco—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Is to wits the ambrosia. See, there Mr. Addison smokes, and writes “Cato.” See there, Mr. Pulteney makes verses like Martial, speeches like Cicero, and smokes—like Mount Etna; while the great Duke of Wharton, who is the duke among wits, and the wit among dukes, has just written an Ode upon Pigtail, in imitation of Pindar!—Drawer, don't forget pipes and tobacco! the strongest Virginia!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Pindar! What's that, I wonder! Something more demoniac than all. Stop! If the Duke of Wharton is here, can't you present me to him? You see I did not get eno' of the other duke this morning.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Not eno' of him! You are a cormorant of dukes, and deserve to be haunted by one.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Hardman's very words! Haunted by a Duke. No such good luck.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.stage: (who has been shaking hands and talking apart with Lord Strongbow, Sir John Bruin, and Colonel Flint; showing, by his bye-play, that he lets them into his plot against Softhead and Easy.)
sp.p: Softhead, I must present you to our boon companions; —my friend, Lord Strongbow (hardest drinker in England); Sir John Bruin, best boxer in England—threshed Figg; quarrelsome, but pleasant: Colonel Flint—finest gentleman in England, and, out and out, the best fencer; mild as a lamb, but can't bear contradiction, and, on the point of honour, inexorable. Now, for the sixth. Ha, Mr. Easy! (I ask him to serve you.) Easy, your hand! So charmed that you've come. You'll dine with us—given up five invitations on purpose. Do—sans cérémonie.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Why, really, my Lord, a plain sober man like me would be out of place—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: If that's all, never fear. Live with us, and we'll make another man of you, Easy!

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: What captivating familiarity! Well, I cannot resist your lordship.
sp.stage: (Strutting down the room, and speaking to his acquaintances.)
sp.p: Yes, my friend Wilmot—Lord Wilmot—will make me dine with him. Pleasant man, my friend Wilmot. We dine together to-day.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Easy invited? La! how flattered he looks,—“asked to serve me,” ha!—I understand—such a sober, steady fellow: never smokes, never drinks, and so despises those who imitate others, that he'll keep me company in shirking that villanous Burgundy, and eschewing that damnable pigtail. Very considerate in Fred.—He's not so bad as he seems.

div.stage: [Softhead retires to the background with the other invited guests; but, trying hard to escape Sir John Bruin, the boxer, and Col. Flint, the fencer, fastens himself on Easy with an air of patronage.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Ah, Mr. Tonson.
Now to serve the dear Duke.) You have not yet bought the Memoir of a late Man of Quality?

sp.speaker: TONSON.
sp.p: Not yet, my Lord; just been trying; hard work.
But the person who has it is luckily very poor; one of my own authors.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: His eye turns to that forlorn looking spectre I saw him tormenting. That must be one of your authors; he looks so lean, Mr. Tonson?

sp.speaker: TONSON.
sp.p: Hush! That's the man; made a noise in his day; David Fallen.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: David Fallen, whose books, when I was but a school-boy, made me first take to reading,—not as taskwork, but pleasure. How much I do owe him!

sp.speaker: TONSON.
sp.p: My lord bows very low! Oh, if your lordship knows Mr. Fallen, pray tell him not to stand in his own light. I would give him a vast sum for the Memoir,—two hundred guineas; on my honour I would!
Scandal, my lord; sell like wild-fire.—I say, Mr. Hardman, I observed you speak to poor David. Can't you help me here?

Lord Henry de Mowbray's Private Memoirs! Fallen has them, and refuses to sell. Love Adventures; nuts for the public. Only just got a peep myself. But such a confession about the beautiful Lady Morland.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Hang Lady Morland!

sp.speaker: TONSON.
sp.p: Besides—shows up his own brother! Jacobite family secrets. Such a card for the Whigs!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Confound the Whigs! What do I care?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: I'll see to it, Tonson. Give me Mr. Fallen's private address.

sp.speaker: TONSON.
sp.p: But pray be discreet, my Lord. If that knave Curll should get wind of the scent, he'd try to spoil my market with my own author. The villain!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Curll? Why, I have mimick'd Curll so exactly, that Pope himself was deceived, and, stifling with rage, ordered me out of the room. I have it! Mr. Curll shall call upon Fallen the first thing in the morning, and outbid Mr. Tonson.) Thank you, sir.
Moody, my Hardman? some problem in political ethics?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Ay, the oldest of all!—the grand social beehive; the toil and the idleness—the bee and the drone.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: And thinking, no doubt, that the bee has the best of it! We may yet toil together, my Hardman.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: This, in you, is new language and noble!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: It comes from Love, the ennobler! You turn away,—you have a grief you'll not tell me—why, this morning I asked you a favour; from that moment I had a right to your confidence, for a favour degrades when it does not come from a friend.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: You charm, you subdue me, and I feel for once how necessary to man is the sympathy of another. Your hand, Wilmot. This is secret—I, too, then presume to love. One above me in fortune; it may be in birth. But a free state lifts those it employs to a par with its nobles. A post in the Treasury of such nature is vacant; I have served the minister, men say, with some credit; and I asked for the gift without shame—'twas my due. Walpole needs the office, not for reward to the zealous, but for bribe to the doubtful. See,
“Noble family to conciliate.” Ah, the drones have the honey!

sp.speaker: WILMOT
sp.p: And, had you this post, you think you could gain the lady you love?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: At least it would have given me courage to ask. Well, well, well,—a truce with my egotism,—you at least, my fair Wilmot, fair in form, fair in fortune, you need fear no rebuff where you place your affections.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Why, the lady's father sees only demerits in what you think my advantages.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: You mistake, I know the man much better than you do; and look, even now he is gazing upon you as fondly as if on the coronet that shall blazon the coach of my lady, his daughter.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Gazing on me?—where?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
