This house, in which you feared to meet infamy, is the home of sorrow and virtue; the home of a woman unsullied, but slandered.—Of her who, loving you still, followed your footsteps; watched you night and day from yon windows; sent you those flowers, the tokens of innocence and youth; in romance, it is true—the romance only known to a woman— the romance only known to the pure! Lord Wilmot is guiltless! He led your child to the arms of a mother!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Silence him!—silence him!—'tis a snare! I retract! He shall not have this girl! Her house? Do I breathe the same air as the woman so loved and so faithless?

sp.speaker: LUCY.
sp.p: Pity, for my mother!—No, no; justice for her! Pity for yourself and for me!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Come away, or you shall not be my child; I'll disown you. That man speaks—

div.stage: Enter Wilmot, Duke, and Lord Loftus.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: I speak, and I prove—
—The Memoirs—
Here is the very letter that the menial informed you your wife sent to Lord Henry. Read it; and judge if such scorn would not goad such a man to revenge. What revenge could he wield? Why, a boast!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY
sp.p: The date of the very day that he boasted. Ha! brave words! proud heart! I suspect!—I suspect!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Lord Henry's confession! It was writ on his death-bed.

sp.speaker: LORD LOFTUS.
sp.p: 'Tis his hand. I attest it.

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: I too, John, Duke of Middlesex, whose word no man ever doubted;—and that is one use of a Duke! And more, sir; my Duchess comes of a race whose sons were all brave, and whose daughters all chaste. She entreats your Lady's friendship; to hold it an honour. Let her name be the answer to scandal. And that is one use of a Duchess.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY
sp.p: Heaven forgive me! Can she? The flowers; the figure; the—How blind I've been! Where is she? where is she? You said she was here! Ellinor! Ellinor! to my arms —to my heart—O my wife!

div.stage: [Exeunt Sir Geoffrey and Lucy into the inner room.

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: My eyes overflow.
Ha! Powers above! Is that the small man once more? Has he betrayed us? Sir, sir, you ought to be half way to France!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD
sp.stage: (who, since the Duke's entrance, has been trying to creep into the earth, now running to HARDMAN).
sp.p: France! Am I to be banished and haunted from my own native country? Mr. Hardman, sir! Mr. Hardman!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: Hush! my lords, destroy this Requisition! When you signed it, you doubtless believed that the Prince you would serve was of the Church of your Protestant fathers?

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: Certainly; we were assured so.

sp.speaker: LOFTUS.
sp.p: Or we never had signed it.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Then you are safe ever more; for your honour is freed. The Prince has retired to Rome, and abjured your faith. I will convince you of this later.

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: What! then perhaps that mysterious small man saved our lives! Sir, sir! He flies me! He gesticulates! A most supernatural small man! Portentous! He awes me!

div.stage: [Duke and Softhead continue to shun each other with mutual apprehension.

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: Glad to find you are not so bad as you seemed, my Lord; and now that Lucy is engaged to Mr. Hardman—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Engaged already? (
So! he asked me here to insult me with his triumph!) Well!

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: Hush, papa! Oh, Softhead, how you wronged that dear Lord Wilmot; who meant so kindly to us too. How dejected he looks!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD
sp.p: Why would you make yourself out such a monster, Fred? Don't do it again. It might take in wiser men than your poor little Softhead.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Never more such gay follies for me! So this then is grief! I never knew it before; how it changes a man!

div.stage: Enter Sir Geoffrey and Lucy: Sir Geoffrey radiant with joy, his form erect, his whole appearance changed.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: I am young! I am young! A load's taken off from my breast. Ha! ha! ha!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: La! is that old Sir Geoffrey? What a laugh! Joy—I suppose! How it changes a man!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Lucy, your parents are united—my promise fulfilled; permit me—

Sir Geoffrey, the son of him who so wronged you, and whose wrongs you pardoned, now reminds you, that he is entrusted with the charge to ensure the happiness of your child! Behold the man of her choice, and take from his presence your own cure of distrust. With his faults on the surface, and with no fault that is worse than that of concealing his virtues;—Here she loves and is loved! And thus I discharge the trust, and ensure the happiness!

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: How!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Peace! Good Hardman, I cannot gainsay you. Her mother has told me already the secret of her heart. Well, well, take her, you—satrap, and never let me see a tear in those eyes; or, in spite of Hardman's rebuke, I will rack you to death with—suspicion.

div.stage: [Duke, Lord Loftus, Easy, Barbara, Softhead, &c., gather round Sir Geoffrey.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Hardman—

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Noble friend!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: How can I accept at the price of—

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Hush! For the third time to-day, you have but one option. You cannot affect to be generous to me at the cost of a heart all your own. Take your right.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Oh, Hardman! I trust I should feel—speak as you, were our positions reversed.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.p: “Tho' our characters differ”—Come, my lord, lest I tell all the world how you bribed the Prime Minister. Say no more, for your own sake.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Oh, name not so paltry a service.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Paltry! 'Tis the power to serve a nation!—On mine honour as man, this is the sole happy moment I have known to-day—the happiest I have known in my war with the world. Here was the true strife; here, between good and evil, the good has prevailed. My life henceforth, is clear. Men I never guessed of, have served me: I will serve men hereafter, as I dreamed that I served but myself: and, faithful still, Lucy, to you, have no bride but my country.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Nay, Lucy, we must not leave him to that mournful fidelity. I have a sister, worthy to replace even your image; and who is already so disposed to admire, that I think she may be pleased to console, him.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD
sp.p: But, indeed, Mr. Easy, I reform; I repent. Mr. Hardman will have a bride in the country—let me have a bride in the city. After all, I was not such a very bad monster.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Pooh. Won't hear of it! Want to marry only just to mimic my Lord.

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: Dear Lord Wilmot; do say a good word for us.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: No, sir; no! Your head's been turned by a lord.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Not the first man whose head's been turned by a lord, with the help of the Duke of Burgundy—eh, Mr. Easy? I'll just appeal to Sir Geoffrey.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: No—no—hold your tongue, my Lord.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: And you insisted upon giving your daughter to Mr. Softhead; forced her upon him.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: I—never!—When?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Last night, when you were chaired member for the City of London. I'll just explain the case to Sir Geoffrey—

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: Confound it—hold—hold! Never hear the end of it!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: And we must claim your promise; because, as you so justly remarked, Mr. Softhead is a jolly old soul! My dear Sir Geoffrey, I say—

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: There—there—that will do. But if ever a lord gets me again into—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: The watchhouse? But you would go, of yourself. “Proudest day of your life.” Sir Geoffrey—

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: Only another wedding on foot, Geoffrey! You like this young reprobate, Barbara?

sp.speaker: BARBARA.
sp.p: Dear papa, his health is so delicate! I should like to take care of him.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: There, go, and take care of each other. Well, Alderman Softhead is a warm man—has a great many votes—and if I should stand for the City? Ha! ha! I suppose it is all for the best.

div.stage: [Duke, takes forth, and puts on, his spectacles; examines Softhead curiously—is convinced that he is human, approaches, and offers his hand, which Softhead, emboldened by Barbara, though not without misgivings, accepts.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Ugh—ugh! Mr. Goodenough Easy. I suspect—I suspect—

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.p: That you've done with suspicion, plagued yourself and all round you quite long eno'. A great deal of dry stuff, called philosophy, is written about life. But the grand thing is to take it coolly, and have a good-humoured indulgence—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: For the force of example, Mr. Easy!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: For the follies of fashion, and the crimes of monsters like myself, and that terrible Softhead!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Ha! Ha!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: For infirmities of temper?

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Ugh!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: When they are but as weather-stains on the oak—that discolour the rind, but mar not the worth of the tree—

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: Good!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: For the pride of a patrician—

sp.speaker: DUKE.
sp.p: Eh!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: When it spreads thro' the heart of a land,—the example of honour!

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: A perfect gentleman, tho' he may not have an ancestor!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: And more than indulgence for the daring plebeian with all his sharp struggles between evil and good, when he fights his way up to fortune, and sees those before him as foes.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.p: Let him, like Hardman, love fame and his country, and I suspect that, like Hardman, he'll be, one day, surprised by his friends.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: My thanks to you both. But alas! my dear Wilmot, many sides to a character!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Plague on it, yes! But get at them all, and we're not so bad as we seem—

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.p: No, Fred, not quite so bad!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.p: Not even poor David Fallen, the Author.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.p: Egad, if the Author himself were here, I should still hope that we might say—‘not quite so bad’—taking us as we stand—Altogether!

div.head: “DAVID FALLEN IS DEAD!” OR, A KEY TO THE PLAY. (AN AFTER-SCENE, BY WAY OF AN EPILOGUE.)
div.stage: SCENE. Wilmot's Apartment.—Wilmot, Sir Geoffrey, Softhead, Easy, and Hardman, seated at a Table. Wine, Fruits, &c.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.l: Well, I've got in my hay.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.l: I should like to have seen him!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.l: By the shock on his nerves—at the sight of a joint. A very great genius—

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.l: I own—now he's dead, That a writer more charming—

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD
sp.l: So THAT is the way that a country is grateful! 'Ere his nerves grew so weak,—if she'd sent him a plateful.

div.stage: [Pause.—Evident feeling that there's no getting over Mr. Easy's paper.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.l: 'Gad, if I were an author, I'd rather, instead, Have the epitaph living—the epigram dead. If Pope had but just reconsidered that matter, Poor David—

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.l: Had gone to the Abbey much fatter!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.l: Let us deem him the Last of a Race!

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.l: But the race that succeeds may have little more pelf—

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.l: Ay; and trials as sharp. I'm an author myself. But the remedy? Wherefore should authors not build—

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.l: No, merchant, their own noble guild! Some fortress for youth in the battle for fame; Some shelter that Age is not humbled to claim; Some roof from the storm for the Pilgrim of Knowledge;—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.l: Not unlike what our ancestors meant by—a College; Where teacher and student alike the subscriber, Untaxing the Patron,—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.l: The son of proud Learning shall knock at the door, And cry This is rich, and not whine That is poor.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.l: Oh right! For these men govern earth from their graves— Shall the dead be as kings, and the living as slaves!

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.l: It is all their own fault—they so slave one another; Not a son of proud Learning but knocks—down his brother!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.l: Yes! other vocations, from Thames to the Border, Have some esprit de corps, and some pride in their order; Lawyers, soldiers, and doctors, if quarrels do pass, Still soften their spite from respect to their class; Why should authors be spitting and scratching like tabbies, To leave but dry bones—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.l: True to the letter. Are their sides, then, so fat, we can't hit on a better?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.l: Why—the sticks in the fable!—Our Guild be the tether,

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.l: Ay: the thorns are rubbed off when the sticks cling together.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD
sp.l: I could be—yes—I could be a Pilgrim of Knowledge, If you'd change Deadman's Lane to a snug little College.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.l: Ugh! stuff!—it takes money a College to found.

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.l: I will head the subscription myself—with a pound!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.l: Quite enough from a friend; for we authors should feel We must put our own shoulders like men to the wheel. Be thrifty when thriving—take heed of the morrow,—

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.l: Where the deuce could they borrow?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.l: Let us think of a scheme.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.l: A scheme! I have got one; the wheel's set a going! A play from one author.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.l: Who'll give you the play? it will not be worth giving. Authors now are so bad; always are while they're living!

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.l: Ah! if David Fallen, great genius, were here—

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.l: A man whom all Time shall revere!

sp.speaker: EASY.
sp.l: The true Classical School, sir! Ah! could he come back!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.l: He'll not be such a fool, sir.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.l: This might do—as a live sort of writer.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.l: Must we take a live man?

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.l: To oblige us he'll be, sir,—as dead as he can!

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.l: With less than your wit, he has more than your leisure. Coquets with the Muse—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.l: Can we get his good side?

sp.speaker: HARDMAN.
sp.l: Yes, he's proud of his order.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.l: As for wit—he has books on his shelves.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.l: By Jove, we will act it ourselves.

div.stage: [Omnes, at first surprised into enthusiasm, succeeded by great consternation.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.l: I'll appeal to Sir Geoffrey. There's one caught already! This suspicious old knight; to his blind side, direct us.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.l: True; and his to suspect us. I rely upon you.

sp.speaker: HARDMAN
sp.l: Me! I have not a minute!

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.l: If the Play has a plot, he is sure to be in it. Come, Softhead!

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.l: I won't. I'll go home to my mother.

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.l: Pooh! monsters like us always help one another.

sp.speaker: SOFTHEAD.
sp.l: Well, I've this consolation— Still to imitate one—

sp.speaker: WILMOT.
sp.l: Let the public but favour the plan we have hit on, And we'll chair through all London,—our Family Briton.

sp.speaker: SIR GEOFFREY.
sp.l: What?—what? Look at Easy! He's drunk, or I dream—
